I have been farming this land since I was a little girl helping my parents, and over thirty years you learn what works in Quzhou. My 4.1 mu is not big, so every corner counts. I plant wheat in the autumn right after the National Day holiday — the whole field goes into wheat because that is what the land is for. I buy improved wheat seeds from the shop in town, the kind everyone around here uses, and I spread compound fertilizer as basal before rotary tilling. I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help the seedlings survive the cold, once at jointing when the wheat starts shooting up, and once at grain filling so the grains are plump. I topdress with urea at green-up and jointing. For pests and weeds, I spray twice — herbicide early and one more time if the aphids come. I expect about 480 jin per mu, maybe a bit more if the spring rain is good.

As soon as the wheat comes off the combine in early June, I plant maize the same day or the next — there is no time to waste in the summer crop. I use hybrid seeds, Denghai or whatever the dealer recommends, and I sow directly without ploughing because the wheat stubble is still fresh. I put down compound fertilizer with the seeder, then topdress with urea when the maize is knee-high. I will irrigate once, maybe twice if July turns dry, because my well can handle it but electricity costs money. Two sprays: one herbicide at seedling stage and one insecticide if the corn borer shows up. If the weather cooperates, I should get around 520 jin per mu. My husband and son work off-farm, so I do most of the field work myself, but my daughter helps during sowing and harvest when the timing is tight.
